USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current tariff pressure ($50B fully in effect) while engaging the newly-resumed low-level trade talks with China. Do not rush to implement the $200B List 3 escalation — use it as leverage while diplomatic channels are open. The US holds the stronger hand and should press for structural concessions on IP theft and forced technology transfer, but a premature jump to $200B risks unnecessary consumer pain and ally alienation.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of -0.3 reflects genuine US leverage. The domestic economy is robust: consumer sentiment hit 100.1 in September (up from 96.2 in August), industrial production is growing steadily at 104.1, and the dollar has strengthened ~6.3% over six months. China, by contrast, is under visible stress — the yuan has depreciated from 6.33 to 6.83 per dollar (~5.4%), signaling capital outflow pressure and Beijing's tacit acceptance of currency weakness to cushion export sectors. China's retaliatory capacity is structurally limited: it can only target ~$130B of US imports versus ~$506B the US imports from China, meaning China runs out of tariff ammunition first (LA Times, Aug 3 2018). China has already retaliated on $50B and announced $60B more, approaching its ceiling.

However, the threat is not purely negative. The $50B tariffs already in effect and the threatened $200B List 3 (now at proposed 25%, comment period closed Sept 5) risk raising prices on consumer goods — the NRF warns American consumers will feel price increases on everyday products (Politico EU, July 11). Industry groups and some Republican senators (e.g., Sen. Hatch) are expressing concern about the broad scope. Tariffs at this scale begin to function as a tax on US consumers and businesses using Chinese intermediate goods.

The action score of -0.15 (leaning toward negotiation, mildly below neutral) reflects the strategic opportunity. Low-level talks are resuming: China's Vice Commerce Minister Wang Shouwen is meeting US Treasury Undersecretary David Malpass in late August (USA Today, Aug 16). These are below the senior level (no Lighthizer or Liu He), suggesting exploratory dialogue rather than a deal framework — but it is the first formal contact since talks collapsed in June. Trump himself told Reuters he doesn't 'anticipate much' from these talks (NPR, Aug 23), which paradoxically creates space: low expectations reduce the political cost of engaging. The US should use this window to test whether China is willing to address structural issues (IP theft, forced tech transfer, Made in China 2025 subsidies) rather than merely offer purchase commitments. The previous May 'deal' that collapsed was essentially purchase promises with no structural reform — that is not worth repeating. Given the strong US macro position and China's weakening hand, patience is the higher-leverage play than immediate escalation.

China under pressure: yuan depreciated 5.4% (6.33→6.83), reserves steady but FX weakening
China retaliation approaching ceiling: ~$60B announced vs US capacity to tariff ~$506B
$50B tariffs fully in effect (List 1 + List 2), List 3 ($200B at 25%) comment period closed Sept 5
Low-level trade talks resuming (Wang/Malpass), first formal dialogue since June collapse
Industry/political pushback rising: NRF, Sen. Hatch warn against broad consumer tariffs
Previous May truce collapsed — purchase-only deals without structural reform are not durable

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain existing retaliatory tariffs for credibility but do not escalate further. Actively pursue negotiations through back-channels and WTO framework while the window remains open before List 3 is finalized. Signal willingness to discuss structural issues (IP protection, market access) without conceding on core industrial policy (Made in China 2025). Use yuan flexibility as a pressure valve, not a weapon.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high (0.55) but not yet existential. The $50B in active tariffs (List 1 and List 2, both at 25%) are significant but manageable — China matched every round and the economy is still growing. However, List 3 ($200B at 25%, up from the original 10% proposed on July 10) would cover roughly half of all Chinese exports to the US and represents a qualitative escalation into consumer goods, threatening business confidence and investment beyond the direct trade impact (JP Morgan's analysis of indirect collateral damage). The yuan's ~7% depreciation since mid-April has partially offset tariff competitiveness losses but Goldman Sachs warns the US may view further weakening as provocation, potentially motivating the rate increase from 10% to 25%. China's WTO complaints (filed July 16, Aug 16, Aug 23) establish legal standing but won't produce results for 18+ months.

The action stance (-0.15, negotiate) reflects the fundamental asymmetry: the US economy is strong (consumer sentiment 100.1, industrial production rising at 104.1, Fed hiking rates) and can absorb escalation pain better than China's export-dependent economy. China cannot win an escalating tariff war — it will run out of US imports to tax before the US runs out of Chinese imports. Further retaliation risks accelerating toward the $450B scenario UBS warned would cause 'damaging economic fallout almost inevitably.' The May truce's collapse (Mnuchin's 'trade war on hold' lasted 10 days) shows neither side can sustain unilateral concessions, but the absence of any negotiating channel since late May is itself dangerous. China should pursue talks not as capitulation but as strategic patience — buying time while WTO processes develop and US domestic political costs of tariff escalation (midterm elections in November 2018) mount.
